rounds.proof_sketch: Input shape [128,1] → size=128, num_blocks=1, block_size=256. Threads 0-127 compute valid hinge loss; threads 128-255 write 0.0f to shared_mem. In reduction stride=128: original has tid<128 (threads 0-127), mutant has tid<=128 (threads 0-128). Thread 128 in mutant accesses shared_mem[128+128]=shared_mem[256] (OOB). This OOB location is NOT controlled by input values—it's uninitialized/padding memory that empirically reads as 0. No input value can change what's at memory location shared_mem[256].
rounds.survival_reason: The mutation causes thread 128 to perform an out-of-bounds shared memory read at index 256 during the first reduction iteration (stride=128). However, this OOB memory location is not influenced by input tensor values—it exists in uninitialized shared memory space beyond the declared array. On the tested GPU hardware, this memory consistently reads as 0.0f, making shared_mem[128] += 0 a no-op. Since shared_mem[128] was already 0 (thread 128's initial contribution), and subsequent reduction steps never observe a difference, the final result remains bitwise identical. Input value changes cannot affect what resides in memory at shared_mem[256] because that location is outside all input-dependent computations.
rounds.kill_strategy: Unkillable under value-only testing. The mutation affects an OOB memory read whose behavior is determined by hardware/runtime memory layout, not input values. To kill this mutant would require either: (1) a configuration change to use size>128 so more threads participate meaningfully in reduction, or (2) different GPU hardware where OOB shared memory reads return non-zero values.
rounds.recommendations: Mutation testing frameworks should flag OOB-dependent mutations as potentially hardware-sensitive and test across multiple GPU architectures. Additionally, the kernel itself has a latent bug—it should declare shared_mem[256+1] or use proper bounds checking to avoid undefined behavior from the tid<=stride case.
